newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul to keep bank ownership limit, bank shrs fall.
newsitem.headline: Seoul to keep bank ownership limit, bank shrs fall.

text.p: South Korean Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik on Tuesday said a four percent ceiling on individual ownership in commercial banks would remain unchanged, sparking criticism from analysts and causing bank shares to dive.
Analysts said the decision had returned discussions on reforming the country's backward financial industry to square one.
"The issue was at the very centre of the reform talks," said Kim Min-tae, an analyst at the LG Economic Research Institute. "By not touching this, all the problems will remain unsolved."
The decision was in contrast to an earlier proposal by the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform to raise the limit to 10 percent under certain conditions.
The news hit bank shares, sending the banking sub-index down 3.9 percent to a session low of 379.58. The index recovered some of the early loss to close down 2.64 percent at 384.64.

"Investors were disappointed in the news the government will not expand the ceiling," said Park Sang-jae, broker at Coryo Securities. "They had anticipated banking shares would come into the spotlight, if the ceiling expansion signals merger and acquisition bids in the banking industry."
Minister Kang told reporters the ministry would instead help establish a responsible management structure at banks by giving big conglomerates a say in the board of directors.

"The government took into account the current situation, such as the relationship between the industrial and financial capital," said Kang. "We expected easing the ownership ceiling would bring about many negative side effects."
He said the top five conglomerates, known as chaebols, would be allowed to have non-permanent directors on the board of directors of banks in which they are major shareholders.
"The source of all the problems at the banking industry was that banks had no owners to take responsibility," said Kim Jin-sang, an analyst at the Seoul branch of Nomura Securities.
"Without addressing that, all the reform measures are nothing but lip service," Kim said.
The ministry is already at the centre of an uproar after it unveiled last week a plan to merge the three financial watchdog bodies and put the unified body under the prime minister.
Union workers at the central Bank of Korea, the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board vowed to walk out if the ministry pressed on with the plan.
Senior officials at the Bank of Korea, to which the Office of Bank Supervision belongs, also demanded that the plan be scrapped and that a fresh debate be launched.
The local financial industry has faced mounting pressure for reforms, especially after a leading steelmaker's collapse in January uncovered a web of corruption.
Hanbo Steel Co, the country's second-largest steelmaker, was declared insolvent after piling up some $5.8 billion of debt to build an integrated steel mill.
The reverberations of the Hanbo failure are still being felt throughout the South Korean economy.
